question.name: Question 19
question.problem:
Consider a function $n(t)$ such that its Laplace transform is $L\{n(t)\}=N(s)$ for $s>{s}_{0}.$ Suppose we wish to find $L\{{e}^{-4t}n(t)\}.$ Select the correct options in the reasoning below.By definition of the Laplace transform, we can write 

$$
\begin{aligned}L\{{e}^{-4t}n(t)\} & ={\int }_{0}^{\infty }{{field-1}}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\infty }{{field-2}}\,n(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={{field-3}}\,\text{for}\,{{field-4}}.\end{aligned}
$$
question.worked_solution:
Starting from the definition of the Laplace transform, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}L\{{e}^{-4t}n(t)\} & ={\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-st}\cdot {e}^{-4t}\,n(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-(s+4)t}\,n(t)\,\text{d}t\end{aligned}
$$

Now, recall that $N(s)={\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-st}\,n(t)\,\text{d}t,$ where $s>{s}_{0}.$ Therefore, 

$$
{\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-(s+4)t}\,n(t)\,\text{d}t=N(s+4),
$$

where 

$$
s+4>{s}_{0}\,⇒\,s>{s}_{0}-4.
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}L\{{e}^{-4t}n(t)\} & ={\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-st}\cdot {e}^{-4t}\,n(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-(s+4)t}\,n(t)\,\text{d}t\end{aligned}
$$

Now, recall that $N(s)={\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-st}\,n(t)\,\text{d}t,$ where $s>{s}_{0}.$ Therefore, 

$$
{\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-(s+4)t}\,n(t)\,\text{d}t=N(s+4),
$$

where 

$$
s+4>{s}_{0}\,⇒\,s>{s}_{0}-4.
$$
